chunks: I said to Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him): 'I heard Hisham ibn al-Hakam narrating from you that God is a body, self-sufficient and luminous, whose recognition is a necessity, which He grants to whomever He wills among His creation.'

So he (peace be upon him) said: 'Glory be to the One Whom no one knows how He is, except He Himself. There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing. He cannot be limited, nor felt, nor touched, nor do the visions comprehend Him, nor the senses, nor can He be encompassed by anything — no body, no image, no lines, no boundaries.'

key_terms.تَحْدِيد: Limitation/bounding — God cannot be assigned any spatial or physical limits
key_terms.تَنْزِيه: Transcendence — the theological doctrine that God is utterly free from all anthropomorphic attributes
key_terms.جِسْمٌ صَمَدِيٌّ نُورِيٌّ: A body (jism) that is self-sufficient (samadi) and luminous (nuri) — the erroneous description attributed to Hisham; the Imam rejects it
key_terms.سُبْحَانَ: Glory be to / Glorified is — a formula of divine exaltation and distancing from imperfection
key_terms.لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ: There is nothing like unto Him — direct quotation of Quran 42:11, the cornerstone of Islamic anti-anthropomorphism

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Sadiq say about describing God as a body or having physical form?
ai.summary: Ali ibn Abi Hamza confronts Imam al-Sadiq (AS) with a report attributed to the eminent theologian Hisham ibn al-Hakam, claiming that the Imam had taught God is a 'self-sufficient, luminous body.' The Imam categorically repudiates this by reciting a powerful declaration of divine transcendence (tanzih), incorporating Quran 42:11 ('There is nothing like unto Him') and emphasizing that God is entirely beyond physical attributes, limitation, sensory perception, and any form of circumscription. This hadith belongs to a pivotal chapter in Kitab al-Kafi's 'Kitab al-Tawhid' dealing with the theological prohibition of anthropomorphism.
